items.title: ULA's Vulcan rocket is set to return to flight on Friday the 13th
paras: Mitigations ULA’s Vulcan rocket is set to return to flight on Friday the 13th This Vulcan launch will be the first to utilize a full complement of six solid rocket boosters.

12 Technicians at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida prepare to install one of the six solid rocket boosters for the Vulcan rocket's upcoming return-to-flight mission. Credit: United Launch Alliance Technicians at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida prepare to install one of the six solid rocket boosters for the Vulcan rocket's upcoming return-to-flight mission. Credit: United Launch Alliance Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav United Launch Alliance announced Wednesday it plans to return its Vulcan rocket to service on November 13, nine months after a solid rocket booster anomaly threw the company’s 2026 launch schedule into oblivion.

The return-to-flight mission will launch 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation, the first of 38 Vulcan flights Amazon has booked to deploy the bulk of its network. The mission will lift off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, and ULA said the launch date is pending range approval.

The launch is critical for ULA after its new flagship rocket suffered nozzle failures on its solid rocket boosters on two of its first four missions, most recently during a flight in February. In both cases, the rocket overcame the nozzle failure and completed its mission, but officials at the US Space Force, ULA’s primary customer, lost confidence in Vulcan.

Space Force officials will closely scrutinize Vulcan’s return-to-flight mission. The Pentagon has entrusted ULA’s Vulcan rocket for roughly half of its major launches through the early 2030s. The Space Force certified the Vulcan rocket for national security launches in 2025, then flew two missions on Vulcan before its grounding after the February booster incident.

In a statement, United Launch Alliance said engineers “made great strides” in understanding the booster anomaly that occurred in February. Engineers “have identified several potential contributors, which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle,” ULA said.

“To support our customers, this upcoming launch will utilize the improved nozzle design, and additional testing and analysis will continue in parallel with the mission,” ULA said. “By flying the improved design, ULA gains valuable flight data that validates these improvements and is the most beneficial path in support of all our customers.”

ULA and Northrop Grumman, the booster manufacturer, have not publicly identified the root cause of the nozzle malfunction in February . Investigators blamed the nozzle problem’s first occurrence in 2024 on a manufacturing defect in an insulator meant to protect the nozzle’s metallic structure from the rocket’s superheated exhaust. Neither company responded to questions from Ars on Wednesday.

The Space Force is counting on United Launch Alliance, a 50-50 joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, to deliver into orbit a backlog of the military’s communications, navigation, missile warning, and surveillance satellites. Amazon Leo, a potential competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink network, also has an inventory of broadband satellites in storage waiting for rides on the Vulcan rocket.

With ULA’s delays, the Space Force has moved six missions off the Vulcan rocket to expedite their launch on SpaceX Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets. ULA received six future missions originally assigned to SpaceX, the military’s other certified launch provider.

The swaps included three GPS satellites that moved off ULA’s Vulcan rocket for launches last year and earlier this year on SpaceX Falcon 9s. Space Systems Command, which oversees military launch acquisition and procurement, also swapped one ULA launch for the Space Development Agency with another on SpaceX.

A launch carrying the Air Force Research Laboratory’s Oracle-M lunar mission will now fly on SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy rocket instead of ULA’s Vulcan, which will receive a future SpaceX-assigned launch in compensation. Space Systems Command completed a similar swap to move a large strategic missile warning satellite from Vulcan to Falcon Heavy.

So far the swaps have had no effect on the number of missions the Space Force has awarded to ULA and SpaceX. The trades are separate from the Space Force’s assignment of unallocated future missions to launch providers, which may already be hamstrung by SpaceX’s plans to retire the Falcon rocket family .

“These swaps are executed in coordination with and with the support of both launch service providers,” a Space Systems Command spokesperson said. “We are grateful for the flexibility shown by our launch service providers during these swaps to help us ensure we can deliver capabilities to the warfighter when and where they are needed.”

Brig. Gen. Eric Zarybnisky, the chief rocket buyer at Space Systems Command, said the military wants to see data from commercial flights on the Vulcan rocket before clearing ULA to resume national security launches. At least two Amazon Leo missions are on the Vulcan launch schedule before it flies another national security mission, perhaps early next year.

“Those flights will have a significant number of solids,” Zarybnisky said. “It’ll depend a lot on what we see, not only on the engineering and tests that we’re doing on the ground, but also what we see from the flight data from the commercial missions they fly.”

The Vulcan launch next month will be the first to fly with a full complement of six solid rocket boosters. The flight will also debut an extended payload fairing to accommodate Amazon’s satellite stack and a shortened Centaur upper stage optimized for low-Earth orbit missions.

items.title: As US ties fray, Europe plans first undersea cable link to Greenland
paras: Out in the cold As US ties fray, Europe plans first undersea cable link to Greenland Europe’s Pan-Arctic Cable will bypass US to link Canada, Japan, and South Korea.

52 European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen (R), Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen (L) and Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen visit Qoornoq in Greenland on September 6, 2026. Credit: Mads Claus Rasmussen / Ritzau Scanpix / AFP via Getty Images) / Denmark OUT European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen (R), Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen (L) and Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen visit Qoornoq in Greenland on September 6, 2026. Credit: Mads Claus Rasmussen / Ritzau Scanpix / AFP via Getty Images) / Denmark OUT Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav The European Union plans to create the first subsea Internet cable directly connecting Europe to Greenland. The Pan-Arctic Cable project could also extend to Canada and eventually link with Japan and South Korea, notably bypassing the United States.

The Pan-Arctic Cable is described as a European Union flagship project in a European Commission joint communication published on October 20, 2026. The policy document describes a new European strategy for the Arctic that supports “a sovereign, secure and resilient submarine cable connection linking Greenland directly to the EU,” while also suggesting that “like-minded partners like Canada” could provide a stepping stone for future cable expansion toward Asia.

“It is interesting that this project is even being considered, because five years ago it would have seemed like not a particularly commercially attractive proposition,” Elisabeth Braw , a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads the Threats to the Global Maritime Order Initiative, told Ars. “But the fact that it’s being considered is very much on trend and a sign of our times.”

The project has gained official support after repeated Trump administration attempts to claim Greenland were finally settled through a trilateral security agreement between the United States, Greenland and Denmark in September 2026. The agreement preserves Greenland’s autonomous territory status within the Kingdom of Denmark while expanding US military access. But relations have grown increasingly strained between the United States and its allies in Europe and Canada since President Trump initiated trade wars with multiple countries and has taken an increasingly pro-Russia stance on the war in Ukraine .

Europe has also been eyeing new Internet cable routes to Asia because more than 90 percent of communications between Europe and Asia run through undersea cables in the Red Sea, according to TeleGeography . Maintaining such cables has become riskier since open warfare resumed between the Yemeni government and Houthi faction this year, with Houthi forces having fired missiles and drones at commercial ships in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait chokepoint and the broader Red Sea.

The Pan-Arctic Cable took shape when European companies and research organizations joined forces with a Greenland telecom operator to sign an agreement on developing the project in 2025, according to Submarine Cable Networks.

Since that time, the project has received European Union backing through the Connecting Europe Facility Digital program. The European Union has already invested $119 million (107 million euros) to “advance Greenland’s secure and sovereign connectivity” along with funding the Pan-Arctic Cable plan, according to the new European Commission policy document on Europe’s Arctic strategy.

But the goal of eventually extending the undersea cable to Japan and South Korea by way of Canada faces considerable challenges, including requiring more European icebreaker ships to support the installation and maintenance of the cable in icy Arctic waters. Multiple pan-Arctic projects have been proposed in the past and some are still in development.

One earlier project known as the Arctic Connect subsea cable aimed to connect Europe and Asia using the Northern Sea Route running along Russia’s Arctic coastline—but that was eventually halted in May 2021 before the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine led to growing Russian isolation from Europe.

Still, the Pan-Arctic Cable is not the only subsea cable project that could strengthen Europe’s ties to friendlier nations. In September 2026, the Norwegian company Bulk Infrastructure Group AS began looking for a Canadian partner to take a majority ownership stake in a new transatlantic cable directly linking Europe to Canada, according to Bloomberg News . That proposed project has been named the Leif Erikson system.

In previous decades, “geopolitics played virtually no role when companies considered where to put their cables and what countries to connect,” said Braw, whose book Undersea War explores why the world has become more dangerous for the Internet’s undersea backbone . But the focus on maximizing data connectivity and Internet traffic has given way to more complex planning that also accounts for international relations and the growing risk of adversaries carrying out surveillance or sabotage of cables.

“We are going to see more cables that connect friendly countries, and then you have to figure out how you can connect friendly countries without going through unfriendly countries’ exclusive economic zones or territorial waters,” Braw told Ars.

Growing international tensions have coincided with suspicious incidents of Russian- and Chinese-linked commercial ships severing European undersea cables in the Baltic Sea by dragging their anchors for long periods of time. In spring 2026, NATO countries’ forces also confronted Russian submarines that were practicing how to disable undersea cables in Arctic waters near Norway, Reuters reported .

Europe’s new Arctic strategy document addresses such security threats by stating that the European Union will establish an Arctic Cable Hub to “monitor, protect and support the repair of submarine cables in the North Atlantic-Arctic.” It also says the European Union will invest in “smart technologies on cables that act as early warning systems for potential threats.”

Such risks for undersea infrastructure are not limited to the Baltic Sea or Atlantic Ocean. In the Pacific Ocean, Chinese-linked commercial ships have also severed undersea cables near Taiwan. Analysts have documented Chinese research vessels spending unusual amounts of time near Pacific undersea cables and warned of the rising risks for US-linked subsea cable projects that are often owned by Big Tech companies such as Google and Meta .

Meanwhile, Iran has threatened to charge fees to subsea cable operators whose cables run through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint. That action comes as part of a broader regional war in the Middle East that began when the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February 2026—and Iran has drawn up plans to potentially attack undersea cables if hostilities ramp up once again.

items.title: Amazon turns its most capable smart speaker into a smart camera, too
paras: Alexa+ Amazon turns its most capable smart speaker into a smart camera, too The Echo Studio with Home Camera can “see and understand what’s in front of the camera.”

26 Credit: Amazon Credit: Amazon Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav Since debuting in 2019, Amazon’s Echo Studio targeted users who wanted superior audio quality from their Alexa-based smart speaker. The latest Echo Studio adds another less-expected differentiator: an integrated camera.

The Echo Studio with Home Camera, released alongside a pile of other Alexa devices today, doesn’t have many audio upgrades over the standard Echo Studio. Each speaker has one 3.75-inch high-excursion woofer and three full-range drivers. They both support Dolby Atmos and Amazon’s proprietary algorithm for adding a surround sound-like effect to stereo audio. Per the devices’ product pages, the speakers have lossless HD audio, Advanced Room Adaptation, and features for fighting noise distortion. Amazon announced the Advanced Room Adaptaion today, saying that the feature “continuously tunes the sound to your space, automatically adapting to the room’s acoustics.”
Both speakers have four-microphone arrays and the same AZ3 Pro processor that Amazon introduced a year ago . The processor has an AI accelerator for using Amazon’s Alexa+ generative AI chatbot .
The devices also have the same dimensions, even though the new Echo Studio With Home Camera fits in a 13MP camera.
The speaker can use the camera to see where you are and adjust audio volume “so your music or audiobook maintains the same volume as you move about.”

Beyond audio capabilities, Amazon sees people using the speaker as a smart camera, allowing them to remotely check on a room in the home to see, for example, “how the dog is doing or make sure you didn’t leave the lights on.”

“Alexa can also see and understand what’s in front of the camera and help you in real time. Pull out a board game box and ask Alexa+ to explain the rules or hold up a cereal box, and Alexa can recognize it and help you reorder more flavors,” Amazon’s announcement says.
One day, users will be able to pair the smart speaker-camera with an Amazon Fire TV for video calls, Amazon’s announcement said, without confirming when.

Like all of our Echo devices, a dedicated button turns off the microphones and any included cameras. There are clear visual indicators whenever Echo devices with a camera are streaming images or video to the cloud to provide transparency—on Echo Studio with Home Camera, a built-in LED turns on. The standard Echo Studio remains available for those who prefer no camera.
Echo Studio With Home Camera users can disable the camera via the Alexa mobile app and “continue interacting with Alexa when the camera is disabled,” the device’s product page says.

Amazon has a notable past when it comes to smart cameras, including previously giving cops access to data from Ring smart cameras without user consent and allegations from the Federal Trade Commission that its employees illegally spied on Ring users (Amazon eventually settled the FTC’s lawsuit for $5.8 million without admitting any wrongdoing). These incidents may lead some privacy-focused customers to opt for camera-less alternatives.

The new gadget indicates where Amazon is going with gadgets since launching Alexa+ in a bid to transform its AI assistant from a money pit into a lucrative tool. With standard Alexa said to have cost Amazon billions of dollars , Amazon’s newest devices aim to boost capabilities for more advanced tasks, especially ones leading to purchases on Amazon’s website or with its partners through Alexa+.
Those added capabilities come at costs that extend beyond potential privacy concerns. The Echo Studio With Home Camera is $250, which is $30 more than the camera-free version.

items.title: Why the world’s first spinal cord transplant is so controversial
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print Shutterstock/PeopleImages The virologist Jonas Salk said that “hope lies in dreams, in imagination and in the courage of those who dare to make dreams into reality”. Salk was certainly daring – he risked paralysing himself, his wife and their children while testing his polio vaccine. Thankfully, it paid off. None of them experienced any ill effects and his work is credited with saving millions .
Risks have to be taken for medicine to advance, and someone is always the first to receive a treatment. But there are risks, and then there are risks.

Salk tested his vaccine on cells, monkeys and children who had already had polio before turning his unexposed family into guinea pigs. His approach is far from standard protocol today, but he did a lot to reduce the risk of something going wrong.

There is less evidence to justify an operation that took place this month in Russia . Details are scant, but the procedure involved cutting out a section of spinal cord from someone with a complete spinal cord injury and gluing in a replacement piece from a donor. The transplant was a world first, but there is little evidence to believe it will have worked or that now was the time to try it.
The transplant was a world first, but there is little evidence to believe it will have worked

History tells us that acting ahead of medical evidence can have catastrophic results. Take the first synthetic organ transplants, which replaced tracheas with plastic tubes. The surgeon who fitted them admitted they hadn’t been tested on large animals because they “didn’t have the time”. Complications and deaths followed .

With new medical procedures, the gold standard is randomised controlled trials, which are costly and take time, but they aren’t the only route. When someone is critically ill, there are compassionate-use protocols that make interventions available before they are fully tested. Pig kidney transplants are currently being trialled this way, for example.

The dream of spinal cord transplants will surely become a reality one day, but only if the science underpinning them is built first. Courage, dreams and imagination are of course good, yet with experimental surgeries, evidence is better.

items.title: The most important part of AI chatbots is being ignored
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print AI chatbots have several layers we don’t always think about Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images ChatGPT was never meant to start a revolution. When it launched in November 2022, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman called it “an early demo” and expectations were low. Personally, my initial reaction was that it seemed no more capable than previous large language models (LLMs) OpenAI had released; it just had a nicer interface. Obviously, I was wrong to dismiss the importance of the interface, but in 2026 I think most people who use AI are making a similar mistake without even realising it. What you think of as ChatGPT or Claude or any other chatbot from a big AI brand is actually many pieces of software wrapped into one, and we are ignoring the most important: the harness.

To understand what a harness is and how it works, it helps to break down the multiple things we call ChatGPT. At the very bottom is the LLM, currently a version of GPT-6, but this gets switched out when OpenAI releases new model families. LLMs do one thing: given a string of text, they predict the most likely next characters. OpenAI’s first model, GPT-1, was released in 2018 as a piece of software that you had to download and run on your computer through a terminal, the text-based interface to a computer that most of us avoid. The same was true of GPT-2 in 2019, until an independent software developer called Adam King created Talk to Transformer, a now-defunct website that allowed you to enter a prompt and get a GPT-2 response in return. Back-and-forth chat wasn’t possible, but this was an early example of an interface, in this case a website, sitting on top of a model.

In 2020, OpenAI released GPT-3 and, for the first time, allowed people to access it through an application programming interface (API), its first commercial product. APIs are a standard way for one computer to communicate with another – for example, Google has a Google Maps API that lets a piece of software send a request for location data. OpenAI’s API let anyone create software that could plug in to GPT-3. At the time, I played with a few of these and found them interesting but clunky – the text they produced was often incorrect or flawed in some way, though it was cool that this level of text generation was even possible. This was essentially still a time of “raw” LLM output, with no guard rails – if you asked GPT-3 to produce hate speech or instructions to build a bomb, it would do so to the best of its ability .

That changed with the release of GPT-3.5 and, at the same time, ChatGPT, which was first called “Chat with GPT-3.5” until a last-minute name change. That original name reveals the way OpenAI saw ChatGPT, as simply an interface to a model, and this explains my reaction as well – the results I got from playing with ChatGPT seemed to be similar to GPT-3, just easier to use.

Actually, there was a crucial difference. With GPT-3.5, OpenAI had attempted to install guard rails that would prevent the model from producing text it deemed harmful, with software that would screen inputs and outputs. These didn’t work very well – you could get around them by asking for a malicious request to be fulfilled in the form of a poem , for example – but this was the beginning of a move away from raw LLMs to ones mediated by a harness sitting between the model and the interface.

Today, the ChatGPT product, whether that’s the app on your phone or the website, has an extensive harness that is mostly hidden from the user. It allows the model to do things like search the internet, read documents, or “reason”, meaning to continuously prompt itself through a “chain of thought” to produce better results. OpenAI also has another, more complex harness for its models, called Codex, which allows the LLM to more directly control a computer and so is particularly useful for writing computer code.

Why does any of this matter? Well, the dirty secret of the big AI firms is that their best models are, to some extent, interchangeable. The technology behind an OpenAI GPT model, a generative pre-trained transformer, is the same as the one used by Anthropic, Google or any other AI company. There are important differences in the data and computing power used to train these models, but generally they are all headed in the same direction, which is why the companies are constantly racing to claim the crown of “best” model before another one takes its place.

What really makes the difference is the harness. To illustrate this, I gave the same prompt – “Who am I?” – to the same model, GPT-6, in three different ways. Via API, I got a response beginning: “I don’t know your identify from this chat.” From chatgpt.com, without being logged in, I got a response that started “That’s a big question. 🙂”. When logged in to my personal account, the response began “You’re Jacob Aron, a senior editor at New Scientist, with a strong interest in mathematics, science, technology and the limits of what we can actually know.”

But the harness matters much more than simply knowing a few facts about the user. In the ARC-AGI test, considered to be one of the leading measures of model “intelligence”, models are tested using either a stripped-down harness that is standardised across all models, or a “provider adapter” that allows access to specific tools each AI firm has built . The difference is remarkable – for GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI’s leading public model, test scores jumped by as much as 80 percentage points when using the provider adapter harness rather than the standard one. For an earlier model, GPT-5.6 Sol, OpenAI found that just tweaking two settings in its harness tripled the resulting ARC-AGI score .

If harnesses are so important, why don’t we talk about them more often? Why don’t AI firms shout about their new harness, rather than just their latest model? I think there are a few reasons. The first is simply that they are complicated and technical – I have taken a whole article to explain them – and your average chatbot user doesn’t really need to know about it. But the second is that they are, in a way, boring. The cost of training a leading LLM is approaching $1 billion, a Herculean effort that requires number crunching across a vast army of computer processors. Once LLMs are trained, we still don’t really know exactly how they produce the results that they do, providing an air of mystery. Harnesses, on the other hand, are just ordinary software, lines of code written by humans that anyone can read.

But here is where it gets really interesting. If a harness is just code, can an AI write and improve its own harness? That is currently an open research question, both inside the AI firms and for academics. For example, in a paper published this August , one research team tested models by identifying repeated failures and proposing tweaks to their harnesses that would address the failures, seeing improvements of around 10 to 40 percentage points on benchmarks. This is why I think we are going to be hearing much more about harnesses in the near future. If the goal of the AI firms is recursive self-improvement – an AI that can build a better AI – then the harness, not the model, could be the key to achieving it.

items.title: Transplanted ovaries adjust to the recipient’s biological age
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print A light micrograph of a section through early-stage follicles, which house immature eggs, in an ovary STEVE GSCHMEISSNER/SCIENCE PHOTO/Getty Images Transplanted ovaries appear to take on the age of their recipients’ bodies. When young mice received ovaries from animals that were past their natural fertility window, the young mice gave birth to healthy offspring. This suggests the younger bodies lowered the molecular age of the older ovaries. Transplanting younger ovaries into older mice also boosted the animals’ overall health , adding to the evidence that ovaries play a greater role in ageing and physiology than we realised.

“Young ovaries lowered the biological age of the brain, liver and uterus in old recipient mice,” says Sharif Iqbal at Harvard Medical School. The discovery follows recent research that found transplanted hearts shift towards the recipient’s age . “An organ’s biological age is not fixed at the time it is transplanted,” says Iqbal. “It responds to the body it lives in. Old hearts became younger in young recipients and old ovaries became molecularly younger in young mice.”
Iqbal and his colleagues used mice of different ages to build an “ovarian clock”, based on levels of gene expression and DNA changes that occur with age.

They then surgically transplanted ovaries between young mice (about 4 months old) and older mice (about 13 months old), which are generally infertile. This gave four combinations: young ovaries in young mice, older ovaries in young mice, young ovaries in older mice and older ovaries in older mice.

Four to five months later, the researchers found that the older ovaries placed in younger mice became molecularly younger, while the younger ovaries in older mice became older. They also observed that being in an older body increased inflammation in the younger ovaries, while a younger body reduced it in the older ovaries.

When the mice mated, four to five months after the transplant, the younger mice with older ovaries gave birth to healthy offspring, says Iqbal. Older ovaries transplanted into different older mice produced no births, he says.

The researchers also found evidence that the age of ovaries impacts the rest of the body. “In a younger body, aged ovaries showed gene and pathway level changes that resemble those caused by treatments known to extend lifespan in mice, such as calorie restriction and the drug rapamycin,” says Iqbal.
A woman’s fertility declines with age, which is often attributed to a fall in egg number and quality, but the environment of the ovaries themselves may also be responsible

Other researchers recently found that ovaries don’t sit inert in the body after menopause, but have an identity shift that may contribute to inflammation . “The ovary is not just a passive reproductive organ. It can influence how other organs age,” says Iqbal.

The researchers hope that understanding which molecular signals made the older ovaries work in the younger mice could lead to treatments that support egg quality and ovarian function in women for longer. Ovary transplants can be carried out due to early menopause or a loss of ovarian reserve following medical treatments like chemotherapy. “If we can identify the signals responsible, it may be possible to mimic a younger environment with treatments [and] without transplantation,” says Iqbal.

Francesca Duncan at Northwestern University in Chicago says the results reveal how plastic ovaries are. “Older ovaries [are] influenced by a young environment and vice versa,” she says. “These results provide important support for therapeutic interventions to extend ovarian longevity.” However, ovarian plasticity can probably only be stretched so far, she says.

items.title: Apple refreshes the iMac, entry-level MacBook Pro with the M6 chip
paras: Routine Refresh Apple refreshes the iMac, entry-level MacBook Pro with the M6 chip Additionally, the N1 chip brings Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.

31 The M6 iMac looks just like the M4 one. Credit: Apple The M6 iMac looks just like the M4 one. Credit: Apple Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav
Apple has announced refreshes for the iMac and the entry-level, 14-inch MacBook Pro . Both machines are getting the M6 chip, which was introduced in the Mac mini several weeks ago.

The M6 is split into two variants for the iMac. Picking the “M6 chip with two Thunderbolt ports” option gets you a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, whereas picking “M6 chip with four Thunderbolt ports” gets you 12 cores for each, instead. The two-port variant maxes out at 24 GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, whereas the four-port one maxes out at 32GB of RAM and 2TB of storage.
There’s only one M6 chip option for the MacBook Pro—the one with the 12-core GPU and CPU. It caps out at 32GB of RAM, but can go to 4TB of storage.

It’s a more substantial refresh for the iMac, as its previous update introduced the M4. Apple skipped the M5 and went straight to the M6 here. In terms of performance gains moving from the M4 to the M6, Apple said with the Mac mini that users can expect up to 40 percent faster CPU performance, up to double graphics performance, and nearly five times faster on-device AI. All that largely matches what we saw when we tested the M6 Mac mini last month, and users of the new iMac should expect similar numbers.
The M6 iMac should see up to double SSD read/write performance compared to the M4 model, too.

The previous entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro had the M5, so that one is just stepping up a single generation. In this case, that means up to 30 percent faster graphics and up to double the Neural Engine performance.

In addition to the M6 chip, both computers now have the N1 chip for wireless connectivity (that means Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6). The iMac is now configurable with up to 2.5Gb Ethernet, while the MacBook Pro still lacks an Ethernet port.

There are no outward design changes to either device; they both look exactly the same as their immediate predecessors. The iMac starts at $1,499 for the two-port version, or $1,699 for the four-port version. The M6 MacBook Pro starts at $1,999.

items.title: South Carolina's measles outbreak jumped to Washington state 5 times in 2 weeks
paras: State to state South Carolina’s measles outbreak jumped to Washington state 5 times in 2 weeks International travel used to be the main risk of measles cases in the US—not anymore.

34 A brightly colored transmission microscope image of measles viruses. Credit: Getty | BSIP A brightly colored transmission microscope image of measles viruses. Credit: Getty | BSIP Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav Since measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, the country’s occasional cases have come mainly from international travelers—visitors from far-flung places where the virus still spreads freely — or unvaccinated US residents who return from abroad with a highly infectious souvenir. But as vaccination rates have slipped nationwide in recent years and outbreaks grow bigger and more frequent, domestic travel now poses a greater risk than international incursions.

In a study published this week in NEJM Evidence, Washington state health officials highlight that risk, detailing how an explosive outbreak in South Carolina reached their distant state through five distinct importation events over two weeks in January. In all, the introductions led to 26 cases among residents before officials stamped out the spread.

South Carolina’s measles outbreak began on October 2, 2025, and was declared over on April 26, 2026. Officials confirmed 997 cases in the state during the outbreak. At the time, it was the largest measles outbreak recorded since the virus was declared eliminated, but Pennsylvania’s ongoing outbreak has since surpassed it.

The study in Washington relied heavily on epidemiological data, linking cases among contacts and exposure sites. But also key to the work was whole genome sequencing, which made clear that cases didn’t just stem from one single introduction of the virus from South Carolina that then spread among Washington residents; instead, it revealed five separate introductions.

“As public health jurisdictions prepare to respond to increased measles importations linked to domestic measles outbreaks, while remaining vigilant for international importations, timely whole-genome sequencing can supplement epidemiologic information to help differentiate distinct importations from local transmission and inform outbreak response,” the authors conclude.

In their analysis, health officials identified the first importation in a resident who fell ill with the telltale rash on January 12 after returning from a trip to South Carolina, where they were exposed to a person sick with measles. Genome sequencing found that the virus closely matched sequences from South Carolina cases. One close contact of the Washington case fell ill and was isolated. No other cases were linked to this importation.

In a second importation event, South Carolina residents visited public places while infectious. As a result, four residents with close contact with the South Carolina visitors fell ill. While infectious, the four residents visited schools, healthcare facilities, and a church. Nine of their contacts and one person exposed in a public location fell ill, leading to a total cluster of 14 cases that spanned January 15 to February 17.

In the third importation event, two state residents returned from South Carolina and fell ill on January 15 to 16. No additional cases were linked to these residents. Similarly, a fourth importation event occurred when a resident returned from travel. The person adhered to isolation and quarantine recommendations, and no cases were linked to this one.

In the fifth importation event, a Washington state resident returned from out-of-state travel where they had contact with ill contacts and fell ill themselves on January 19. While contagious, they visited a school and a healthcare facility. Six close contacts fell ill. In all, this cluster of seven cases spanned January 19 to January 29. The genome sequences from five of the cases were nearly identical to those seen in South Carolina.
Officials credit basic public health work of quarantines, isolation, and contact tracing with keeping the virus from spreading farther than it did.

While the study highlights how readily this virus can spread among states amid declining vaccination, it also contradicts a common talking point from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Kennedy, a prominent anti-vaccine advocate, has downplayed the current measles surge in the US and aggressively defended against suggestions that his decades of anti-vaccine misinformation and disinformation have contributed to the surge in cases and drop in vaccination.

Instead, Kennedy claims that there is a “global outbreak” and the US is “doing a better job than any country in the world at controlling the measles outbreak.” Both claims are false . Dozens of other countries have lower case rates than the US. While some countries, including neighboring Canada and Mexico, are also seeing large increases in cases, the soaring case tally in the US is not being driven by international imports, but by domestic spread in under-vaccinated communities.

According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , only 18 of the country’s 4,588 confirmed measles cases this year were reported among international visitors. Of all the cases, 4,404 (96 percent) are linked to a domestic outbreak. The US has had 43 new outbreaks this year.

items.title: Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware threatens most servers on planet Earth
paras: BREAKING THE CHAIN OF TRUST Code-execution flaw in UEFI firmware affects most servers on planet Earth Critical flaw in EDK2 allows attackers to execute code early in the boot process.

21 Credit: Getty Images Credit: Getty Images Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav Defenders across the world face the burden of responding to yet another botched code-execution vulnerability, this time in boot-time firmware used by most of the world’s server vendors and data centers.

The vulnerability, with a severity rating of 9.5 out of 10, resides in the TianoCore EDK II , an open source codebase that hardware makers and cloud providers use to create the UEFI firmware that runs during the boot-up sequence. Last year, a representative of the UEFI Forum called EDK2 the “preeminent solution / implementation of the UEFI specifications.” Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively. Project Mu, Microsoft’s hardened EDK2 fork, used the code containing the vulnerable component as well.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, is a memory-corruption flaw in an ICMP component that attackers can exploit to execute malicious code that runs before the operating system and firmware can implement defenses like Secure Boot , which establishes a chain of trust for all code, including the Trusted Platform Module (TPM), loaded during boot. While final payloads delivered by CVE-2026-97631 have no persistence—meaning they run only once—they can give attackers a wide opening to install other payloads that also run each time early in the boot process.

The parties that discovered CVE-2026-97631—Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google—had arranged for it to stay under wraps until a coordinated disclosure that was scheduled for January. AMI, a maker of motherboards and other hardware, published this pull request last month that detailed the vulnerability and included a code fix. Once the post came to the attention of the discovering parties, TianoCore Project members published a public advisory last week.

With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits. Further compounding the urgency, patching UEFI code vulnerabilities in millions of end devices sold and used by thousands of hardware makers and cloud providers is cumbersome and time-consuming. Word of the vulnerability comes six days after another botched disclosure, this one involving a critical code-execution vulnerability in the PHP programming language.

“This vulnerability in the ICMP parser of the EDK2 network stack is interesting in terms of how it affects the chain of trust and the broader ecosystem,” said HD Moore, creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at security firm Dragos. “An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint’s TPM. This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario).”

CVE-2026-97631 is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe), which is responsible for allowing servers, storage equipment, and other devices to boot using code downloaded from a local network. During this process—known as the pre-execution environment boot—the driver uses a network listener to monitor for ICMP errors. Because the driver doesn’t enforce a memory copy limit of 504 bytes, overwriting adjacent data, a malicious insider or a hacker who has gained low-level access to a local network can send an error message that appends code past this limit. The IUEFI module running on the CPU then becomes corrupted.

During network boot, the PXE Base Code driver (NetworkPkg/UefiPxeBcDxe) keeps a receive request open for ICMP error messages and copies each received message into the fixed 504-byte field Mode.IcmpError of its private context structure. The copy loop’s bounds handling is incorrect in both the IPv4 and IPv6 handlers (PxeBcIcmpErrorDpcHandle and PxeBcIcmp6ErrorDpcHandle): for a message longer than 504 bytes it still copies bytes into the field, and it advances the destination pointer by the cumulative rather than the per-fragment length, so an oversized message writes attacker-controlled bytes past the field. Nothing earlier on the receive path restricts the message length.

The malicious error can be delivered through a simple unicast sent from any network distance to a target device’s IP address, as long as it’s sent during the PXE boot sequence. An attacker can deliver a denial-of-service by causing the boot sequence to hang. When the attacker knows what the target firmware build is, it can plant a “counterfeit event” that executes the malicious code on the CPU in its UEFI firmware environment. The code runs in ring 0, a CPU’s most privileged execution level. Because exploits bypass attestation processes designed to cryptographically prove to remote servers that the hardware is secure, they present a key opportunity for elevating limited privileges.

CVE-2026-97631 joins a long list of previously discovered vulnerabilities in UEFI or code that works closely with it. The most severe of them, LogoFail , stemmed from logo images included in the UEFI of just about every hardware maker. Rendering bugs allowed attackers to subvert the chain of trust UEFI enforces and go on to install malicious components before the OS loaded or Secure Boot ran. PixieFail was a vulnerability similar to CVE-2026-97631. It, too, was the result of faulty PXE boot flaws in EDK2. Following discovery of the vulnerability, researchers embarked on multiple fuzzing projects designed to surface other critical flaws in the open source code library. It appears those efforts failed to find this latest flaw.

Like CVE-2026-97631, exploitation or use of these payloads is appealing because it allows attackers to infect machines early in the boot process, before TPM and other defenses load, so they can inflict maximum damage. Given the ubiquity of CVE-2026-97631, Moore said it’s likely a “forever” bug that will live on in end-of-support systems.

There are important caveats and limitations to exploiting this latest vulnerability. As noted, some level of control over a local network is a prerequisite. That likely limits exploitation to insiders or attackers, such as nation-states or ransomware operators, who manage to gain low-level access inside a network and are looking for a way to elevate system rights. There’s no evidence yet that CVE-2026-97631 provides an initial entry point into a network. There are other hurdles to clear.

“For exploiting the vulnerability itself, an attacker needs to guess specific addresses within the target system, so it’s not something that you can throw a single exploit at any target and get RCE across a diverse range of devices, but it needs to be tuned for each target model/version/configuration since the addresses will change based on those,” Jesse Michael, a principal researcher at firmware security firm Eclypsium, told Ars. “Unlike some of the previous, high-profile vulnerabilities like BootHole, Black Lotus, and Baton Drop, this vulnerability can be fixed with a basic code fix, which will require deploying a BIOS/UEFI update, but they don’t need to deal with revocations, pk/kek/db/dbx key management updates, or making sure to update OS and provisioning media like you do with Secure Boot bypasses in the bootloader itself.”

CVE-2026-97631 doesn’t affect home and small office users, or any other users who boot their devices solely from disk drives. Instead, it applies only to organizations with machines that boot from local networks, or conceivably from Internet-connected resources. Even then, the targeted firmware must rely on EDK2, as opposed to a different reference implementation, and use the PXE functionality (which is turned on by default).

In an email, Intel said that none of its “commercial products currently under security support” are known to be affected. “Intel does not include the affected EDK2 functionality in its reference code, though it may be integrated by an OEM board vendor or system manufacturer,” the company added. It advised customers to check with their system manufacturer for specific guidance. Publicly available Intel reference code , however, makes reference to EDK2. Further, TianoCore has said that each Intel-supplied UEFI development kit “is a fully validated implementation… for a specific revision of the EDK II source.” Many other Intel documents reference EDK2 as well.

Arm, meanwhile, responded to a list of questions with: “CVE-2026-97631 is not directly applicable to Arm’s product portfolio.” Like Intel, firmware the company makes available also borrows heavily from EDK2. TianoCore has also documented Arm’s reliance on EDK2.
While it’s possible some platforms are free of EDK2 code, it’s prudent for users of all servers to investigate if CVE-2026-97631 affects them.

Questions sent to AMD, Phoenix Technologies, AMI, Microsoft, and Amazon—likely some of the other biggest organizations affected—went unanswered when this post went live. Without concrete answers to questions about the use of EDK2 by organizations like these, it’s impossible to say what or how devices are affected and what actions, if any, these organizations, or their users, should take. Representatives from the TianoCore Project also didn’t respond.

Some readers are likely to be unhappy at the lack of detail. Sometimes—particularly in cases involving botched disclosures that break embargoes months before they’re scheduled to lift—there’s no escaping the lack of actionable information in initial reporting.

Those affected should check with the maker of the firmware being used to boot their systems and ask for guidance. Beyond that, they should consider turning off network boot capabilities at least temporarily if possible. Firmware configurations should always enable security features such as TPM and Secure Boot whenever possible, although those defenses don’t protect against this particular threat. It’s also a good idea to monitor logs for signs of exploitation attempts.

This victory meant a lot to the Swiss, who had been a ball boy there in 1993, and had already finished runner-up twice in front of his home crowd back in 2000 and 2001.

Friendships are built by repeated contact, not by being liked
items.hook: This is the single most useful fact in the whole guide.
paras: Studies of primary-school classrooms found that children seated next to each other were far more likely to become friends than children seated across the room. When teachers changed the seating, new friendships formed with the new neighbours.

So the engine is: same place, same people, same activity, over and over. The day at the yo-yo bar followed by basketball is that engine working - shared activity changed how the other boy treated him. It was not luck.
items.do: Pick one activity he already likes and commit to it weekly for a full term.

items.title: Keep the proximity - change the watching
items.hook: Your instinct is half right, and the other half matters.
paras: You are right that being around the group matters: children nominate as friends the children they see and interact with most. 'Out of sight, out of mind' is real for acquaintances.

But guidance written for schools is blunt: merely remaining beside a group is not friendship. A child who hovers is read as a bystander rather than a player, and it holds him in the one-down position. Watching has a use - but only as the first twenty seconds of joining in, never as the endpoint.
items.do: Keep telling him to stay near the group. Add: 'then take a job in the game'.

items.title: Teach 'watch, then blend'
items.hook: The best way to join a game is not to ask.
paras: Most of us were told to walk up and say 'Can I play?' But that makes everyone stop and look at him, and makes 'no' very easy.

The better sequence, used by people who study play: watch for about twenty seconds to learn the game and where the line is, then slide into the action without stopping it. Take the end of the line. Stand in the outfield. Pick up the ball and pass it back.
items.do: Rehearse it at home in five minutes. Ask him to name the 'easiest job' in each game.

items.title: Host one friend at a time - this is the biggest lever you control
items.hook: The child who invites is rarely short of friends.
paras: Pick a child he has had fun with in the last month, not someone he admires from afar. Invite one person for one to two hours. Put away anything precious, have two activities ready, start with a snack, and let the guest choose sometimes.
Keep it short and end while they are both still enjoying it. Then leave a few weeks before inviting the same child again, so the invitation can come back to him.
items.do: Text one parent this week and set a date for the school holidays.

items.title: Ask the teacher one specific question
items.hook: Teachers see the playground. Ask them to name names.
paras: Ask two things: who does he play well with, and could he be seated near them or paired with them for group work?
Seating is one of the few levers that reliably creates new friendships, and it is invisible to the children - no one has to know it was arranged.
items.do: Email the teacher this week with those two questions.

items.title: Do not push into a group that is rejecting him
items.hook: Here the advice is the opposite of persistence.
paras: Where a group is actively excluding him, the guidance is to back off - when you back off from people, they can move towards you. Put his energy into two or three other children instead of one closed circle.
Friends in more than one place - school, a club, family friends - also make him far less vulnerable when one group turns cold.
items.do: Help him list three children outside the difficult group he could get to know.

items.title: One or two good friends is the goal - not popularity
paras: Kids need one or two good friends. You do not need to worry about him being the most popular child in the class.
His warmth and kindness are already the raw material. Treat this as coaching a skill, not fixing a fault - if he feels like a project, he will resist.
items.do: Say his strengths out loud, often. Confidence is what carries a child into a group.

items.title: Playing and talking with girls is normal and good
items.hook: Children believe gender matters far more than it actually does.
paras: In one large classroom experiment, simply seating boys and girls next to each other doubled how often they became friends.
Girls' play tends to build conversation, turn-taking and inventing games together; boys' play builds bigger, faster group play. Being good at both widens his circle.
items.do: No action needed. Just do not let him think it is odd.

items.title: When to get more help
items.hook: Ordinary friendship difficulty is not a disorder.
paras: Get more support if he becomes reluctant to go to school, is persistently distressed, has changes in sleep or appetite, or says it is happening all the time and he cannot make it stop.
Start with his teacher, then the school counsellor, then your GP for a referral. Kids Helpline is free and open 24/7 on 1800 55 1800, for children and for parents.
items.do: Save Kids Helpline in your phone: 1800 55 1800.
